Earing
EER-ing
noun
Not from the ear of corn nor the ear of the head, but from the old verb to ear — Old English erian, akin to the Latin arare, “to plow.” Earing is plowing; earing time is the season of tillage.

Biblical Definition

Earing in the KJV is plowing. It comes of the old verb to ear, from the same root as the Latin arare, to till and turn the ground; it has nothing whatever to do with the ear of corn or the ear of the head, and the modern reader who supposes Genesis speaks of the heading of grain has lost the whole sense. Joseph tells his brethren the famine has five years yet to run, “in the which there shall neither be earing nor harvest” (Gen 45:6): no plowing and no reaping, the year’s whole round of labour struck out at both ends, seedtime and ingathering alike suspended under the hand of God. Samuel warns Israel that the king they demand will set them “to ear his ground, and to reap his harvest” (1Sa 8:12) — the free husbandman reduced to plowing another man’s field. The elders bring the heifer down to a rough valley “which is neither eared nor sown” (Deu 21:4), ground the plow has never touched. But the word’s weight falls in the restating of the fourth commandment: “Six days thou shalt work, but on the seventh day thou shalt rest: in earing time and in harvest thou shalt rest” (Exo 34:21). The LORD names the two busiest hours of the farming year and commands the sabbath in both by name. Precisely where the argument for working is strongest — where the ground is ready, the weather turning, the crop standing — there the command to rest is spoken again.

Webster 1828 Definition

Plowing; tillage. From the old verb “to ear,” to plow — not from the ear of corn.

EARING, plowing; the tilling and turning of ground.

From the verb to ear, Old English erian, akin to Latin arare, “to plow.”

It has no kinship with the ear of corn nor with the ear of the head.

Earing time is the plowing season, one of the two busiest of the year.

In earing time and in harvest thou shalt rest (Exo 34:21).

Key Scripture

Gen 45:6 — "For these two years hath the famine been in the land: and yet there are five years, in the which there shall neither be earing nor harvest."

Exo 34:21 — "Six days thou shalt work, but on the seventh day thou shalt rest: in earing time and in harvest thou shalt rest."

Deu 21:4 — "And the elders of that city shall bring down the heifer unto a rough valley, which is neither eared nor sown, and shall strike off the heifer's neck there in the valley:"

1Sa 8:12 — "And he will appoint him captains over thousands, and captains over fifties; and will set them to ear his ground, and to reap his harvest, and to make his instruments of war, and instruments of his chariots."

Modern Corruption

The word is misread as the heading of grain; and the sabbath it guards has been surrendered to productivity, which is the deeper corruption.

expand to see more

There is a live corruption here, and it is not the lexical one. The fourth commandment names earing time and harvest — the two hours of the farming year when a man could most plausibly plead necessity — and commands rest in both. Our age has learned to plead that necessity fifty-two weeks a year. Work has been promoted into the room of worship: the crowded calendar is worn as a badge of seriousness, busyness is mistaken for faithfulness, and the man who keeps the Lord’s day whole is reckoned a man who does not care whether his family eats. But the LORD who gave the harvest gave the day, and He commanded the rest at the very hour the plow was heaviest. To work through the sabbath because the season is urgent is not diligence; it is unbelief with calluses on its hands.

The principle to recover is that the sabbath is not the wage of finished work but the gift of a finishing God. Israel rested in earing time while the ground still wanted plowing, and in harvest while the grain still stood in the field, and the LORD fed them. The rest God commands does not wait upon the field being done, because the field is never done; it comes on the seventh day and calls a man off the plow whether he thinks he can spare the hour or not. That is the whole discipline of it: the rest is commanded when it costs, so that the resting is faith. He who will not lay down the mattock one day in seven has made the harvest his god, and the harvest is a hard master that never once says “enough.”

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means plowing, tillage — from the old verb “to ear,” to plow.

expand to see more

Earing — from the verb to ear, Old English erian, “to plow.”

It is kin to the Latin arare, “to plow,” and not to the ear of corn.

Earing time is the plowing season, the first hard labour of the year.

Neither earing nor harvest: the famine struck out both ends of the year (Gen 45:6).

In earing time and in harvest thou shalt rest (Exo 34:21).

Usage

"Earing is plowing, not the heading of grain — the old verb to ear means to till."

"Five years of neither earing nor harvest: the famine took the seedtime and the reaping together."

"In earing time and in harvest thou shalt rest — the sabbath is commanded at the busiest hour."
